study.title: Leviticus 15 - Body impurities, ritual separation and path of purification
study.overview: Leviticus 15 gathers instructions on ceremonial impurities linked to bodily flows in men and women. The chapter does not first deal with moral guilt, but of states of impurity that prevented access to the sacred and demanded separation, washing, waiting until the afternoon and, in certain cases, offering in the sanctuary. The text emphasizes that the holiness of God cannot be treated with carelessness: that which is unclean must not contaminate the tabernacle. At the same time, the chapter shows that there is provision of restoration; impurity is not necessarily definitive, for there is a path of purification and return to ritual communion.

outline.title: Abnormal flow in man and his purification
outline.explanation: The chapter begins with a case of correction that makes the man unclean and contaminates objects and people by contact. Impurity spreads by bed, seat, seal, hands, bowls and any close contact. When the flow ceases, the restoration requires a count of seven days, wash in living waters, and on the eighth day two birds as a sin offering and burnt offering, with purification before the LORD.

outline.title: seminal emission and sexual contact
outline.explanation: Here appears a distinct case: the seminal spill makes the man unclean until the afternoon, and all that touches becomes unclean until the afternoon. If there is sexual intercourse, both wash and remain unclean until the afternoon. The text distinguishes this situation from the previous pathological flow, showing that not all body impurity has the same origin or requires the same rite.

outline.title: Menstrual flow and prolonged flow of blood
outline.explanation: The chapter treats the woman in her menstrual cycle and also blood flow out of the usual time. In both cases there is separation, contact contagion and need for purification. If the flow extends beyond the custom, the woman continues unclean as long as the condition lasts and, upon ceasing, counts seven days before offering two birds in the sanctuary for purification.

outline.title: Synthesis: Protect the tabernacle and order the life of the people
outline.explanation: The conclusion interprets all norms as a means of separating Israel from its impurities so that it does not die in defiling the tabernacle of God. The final verse summarizes the covered cases: flow in man or woman, menstruation and relationship with unclean woman. The law acts as ritual protection and as a teaching of reverence in the face of divine presence.

study.context: The chapter is inserted in the Levitical instructions on purity and holiness. The text itself speaks of the tabernacle of the testimony, showing that the central concern is the coexistence of the people with the presence of God in the midst of the camp. Notes indicate that body impurities were treated as states of ceremoniality, linked to weakening or body condition, and not necessarily direct moral sin. The text also differentiates situations: abnormal flow, seminal emission and menstruation are not all treated in the same way.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that the holiness of God reaches even the daily bodily life. Not everything that is natural is treated in the same way: there are normal situations that generate ritual impurity and there are abnormal flows that require a longer process of purification. The point does not seem to be that the body is bad, but that human fragility, the loss of fluids and the condition of impurity signal disorder in relation to the pattern of integrity and the holy presence of God. The chapter also shows a contagion logic: impurity goes through contact and requires concrete separation measures. At the same time, there is ritual grace in the provision of purification; the unclean is not excluded forever. An evangelical reading can see here the contrast between divine holiness and the insufficiency of external means to produce definitive inner purity, without erasing the pedagogical and historical value of these norms for Israel.

scholarViews.insight: Notes distinguish the abnormal flow from the case of semen emission; the first is understood as something pathological and contaminating, while the second receives a simpler, washing and impurity treatment until the afternoon.

The commentator reads the female impurities as ceremonial, covering both the regular flow and the pathological excess, and highlights that the woman touched by this condition became unclean and needed purification.
The final note summarizes the function of the law: to separate Israel from their impurities to prevent the people from profane the tabernacle and to suffer judgment by approaching unclean.

questions: What kind of reverence does God's holiness require in the most common things in bodily and domestic life?
How does this chapter help distinguish between ritual impurity in the Old Testament and personal moral guilt?
How does the provision of purification point to the need for restoration before God?
study.practice: This chapter invites practical reverence: to treat worship, body and community life seriously before God. In Christian application, he reminds us that outer purity does not replace inner transformation, but also that God takes seriously the way we approach him. It is worth examining whether there are areas of life in which we trivialize what defiles, and practicing repentance, discipline, prudence and respect for the holiness of the Lord in the home, in worship and in human relations.
study.uncertainty: The grades provided offer historical and medical interpretations on some points, but the chapter does not directly explain the cause of all flows. Therefore, it is not safe to state more than the text and notes allow, especially on specific diagnoses, external customs or unmentioned historical details. There is also limitation in the notes of Matthew Henry, whose excerpt about verse 19 is incomplete; the synthesis here uses only the clearly present meaning in the given excerpt.
